utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Martinovic and Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Before you have the re-examination of the witness, Mr. Scott, there is one thing I would like to mention to both parties. We just got informed by the registrar that the medical examination of Mr. Naletilic has been postponed due to the scheduling difficulties regarding the transportation arrangements. We are very sorry about this delay, but we are ensured that the examination will take place as soon as possible. We are expecting the report from this medical examination very soon. So, Mr. Scott, your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, just a couple of questions actually on further review from last week. Just to confirm in light of some of the questions on cross-examination, in a number of instances, did you and, to your knowledge, others doing similar work as you, find multiple copies of, for instance, the same document in different files or parts of the Zagreb archive?

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And a similar question but a bit different: Was it also the case that you often found related or connected documents, not the same document, for instance, a response or a reply to one document? Did you often find related or connected documents spread among a number of different files?

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, also very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if the usher can assist me, if the witness can please be shown the Selected Zagreb Documents binder that has been used with this witness, and specifically Exhibit P603.1. Perhaps it might be easier if we could put that -- just put that on the ELMO. Might prevent everyone necessarily having to dig that document out. Mr. Usher, if you can put the English version of Exhibit P603.1 on the ELMO, please. And Mr. Prelec, if you can look at that for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: in your testimony last week that one of the things that you considered is the external consistency or corroboration of a document. If you knew that there was, for instance, trial testimony that was the same as or consistent with a document, would that have an effect on your view as to the authenticity of a document?

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And my final question to you is this: You were asked by Defence counsel, in some respects, to express an assessment over the authenticity of particular documents or a view as to particular documents. My question to you is, based on your extensive work and the work of others with whom you're closely associated at the archive, were you able to make an assessment as to the identification and authentication of the archive as a whole? In other words, do you have a view that it is what it purports to be, that is, the HVO archive?

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm certain it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again, briefly, can you explain to the Chamber why you believe that.

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be -- I think I may have put this actually in a prior answer. But it would be impossible to create something like the archive, or a substantial portion of it, in any fashion other than the fashion in which such things are normally created, which is to say by the day-to-day business of a very large political and military organisation over the space of several years. Well, I could maybe put it this way: As an historian, I'm not aware of any case ever in recorded history of something of this nature, something of this size being called in question in the way that you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Prelec, I thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. I would make a further record, please, as to the documents tendered through this witness. Your Honour, the so-called Zagreb Archive Documents are listed in what has separately been marked for identification for ease of reference and for the record as Prosecution Exhibit P883. It is a 26-page list, and obviously it would consume a substantial amount of time if I were to read all those numbers into the record, but P883 is a listing of that portion of that document tendered through Mr. Prelec. In a similar fashion and as provided to the Chamber last week -- the Chamber should have all these lists available to it. They were provided to your staff last week. There are also an additional five Zagreb documents among the so-called International Armed Conflict binders. Those are separately on another list, but for the record, they are short so I can do it rather quickly. IAC19, IAC38, IAC64, IAC65, and IAC67. There is a third set of documents which are titled - and again a listing that is available to the Chamber - UNPROFOR, (BiH Command Kiseljak), and I won't mention the rest of the title because it's a private session or an under-seal matter, but that document -- that list then indicates a number of documents starting with P205.1 and concluding that list at P569. Those are tendered to the Chamber at this time. There was a fourth bundle of documents which I have simply for my own purposes labelled as the Vance-Owen bundle, which is -- again a list has been provided to the Chamber, but they are IAC27, IAC28, IAC29, P239, P239.1, P265.1, P271, P272, and P349. I have also provided to the Registry for its assistance a list of those documents specifically mentioned by number in the course of Mr. Prelec's direct examination, and that is also available. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections from Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. The Defence for Mr. Mladen Naletilic will object, and we will do that within 30 days in writing, to those documents which we do object to, and we will also inform the Court which ones we do not object to. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I understand especially in that Vance-Owen bundle there are some documents of the Resolutions of the United Nations which -- do you still object to those documents into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, right now, I would tell you no on the Vance-Owen. On the United Nations documents, we would not object to those, and we will also put that in writing. There are so many documents in the one binder that we would like to have the time to look through each one and make a decision. But for the Vance-Owen documents, the United Nations documents, the Defence of Mr. Naletilic has no objection to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. The Defence of Vinko Martinovic so far has no objections to these documents, but we reserve the right later on to perhaps challenge some specific documents, but so far we have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since we have so many documents tendered by the Prosecution, I believe that the Defence counsel have 30 days to submit your written objections concerning those documents. At the same time, I also believe that we have to do some reform about the submission of the objections on a single document or few documents. We believe that for a single document, there is no need for the 30 days to submit the written objections. So later on, if there is a single document or very few documents, both parties will have seven days to submit their written objections so that -- to ensure a fair and expeditious trial. Thank you. Any questions from Judges? Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, can you assist me on this: Are there internationally recognised rules and norms for, first, for keeping materials and then archiving them? In other words, was there much difference between the procedures followed in the former Yugoslavia from the ones followed when you were carrying out your research in Yale or Harvard?

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are such norms, and I do know that they are currently implemented in Croatia and specifically with regard to this particular collection, although I don't know when this practice began. I can say that my prior experience in archives in Croatia, which would date to the early 1990s, they didn't seem particularly different, but I'm a user of archives, not a technician, so I don't actually know the specifics, the specific rules. I do know they exist, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I put it this way: Was there much difference between the methodology of archiving for your doctorate in relation to early nationalism and later archiving of the HVO papers?

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say no. It was similar in that there was a cataloguing system, and there's a -- there are means of preservation. It has become Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. much more important for older or physically sensitive documents. But no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So can I take it that if you were carrying out research in, say, the former Communist Russia and pre-Communist Russia and Czarist Russia, that there would be some similarity in the archiving of materials?

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think so. I have not actually worked in either of those, but yes, I would think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Really, the point of all this is, is there an internationally accepted method of archiving? And you have answered my question, that an historian can go from one continent to the other and feel comfortable with the methodology.

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. The other thing I wanted to ask you about, on the basis that there are internationally accepted rules for archiving, if one were dealing with state documents, is it accepted fairly widely that sensitive state documents are not available to researchers before a certain period has elapsed? In Britain and Ireland, we have the 30-year rule, the 50-year rule, and the 100-year rule. For instance, it would only be 'round about now that documents in relation to very sensitive treaty negotiations during the First World War would be totally open to historians. Did you come across that sort of rule in relation to sensitive state papers?

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly that's a very common practice. Every state has its own rules, and they vary from state to state. With regard to the material now in the archive, what we have been calling the HVO archive, our access to that -- our access to that is an exception to that rule because the user is ultimately a Court, the Tribunal. It's a legal proceeding. They're not for the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So the same rules didn't apply.

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, we have specific permission from the government. And by "government," I mean the Cabinet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The other thing I was going to ask you is was the existence of that type of rule -- could the existence of that type of rule be an explanation for the absence of any President Tudjman papers, which I think Mr. Meek put to you, or it might have been Mr. Par, on Friday.

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those are in a different location. The HVO archive consists almost entirely of material coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Croat entity there. The Tudjman papers would be and are, indeed, in the custody of the Republic of Croatia and always have been. They have not, to my knowledge, been yet submitted to the Croatian archive. They should be still in the office of the president. There are, then, further regulations for when -- after how long, and I know -- I've looked into Croatian legislation on this -- how long government offices should retain different classes of papers. Ultimately, they do end up, yes, in the archive, but they won't -- they shouldn't go into this particular collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So it was no surprise to you, as a researcher and historian, not to find Tudjman papers in this particular archive?

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, to bring you specifically to this case, as you've spent quite a while with these archives, you must have become aware of the existence - and you mentioned them, indeed - of independent special units within the HVO. And the evidence in this case has been that Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Martinovic were involved in independent special units. Could you -- is it within your competence to help us with these independent special units? Were they independent of army control or independent of each other, or what do you mean by "independent special unit"? If you feel this is outside your area of expertise, I mean, I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give perhaps a very limited answer, which would be based on just general research in this area, since I haven't made a study of the units, per se.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is there are two, I suppose, categories that one could consider. Independent units as independent -- or rather, as not part of the ordinary traditional military hierarchy, which is in some ways similar across a broad range of armies, from a central command, main staff, all the way down to a platoon or a squad. So a unit that is within the army, but outside the structure that the rest of the army has. It's often said that these units, for example, are, you know -- I don't speak now specifically about this case -- are assets of the general staff or the central command. The other thing I could say is there's a class of units that were referred to as anti-terrorist units. And this covered also a certain range. It was the practice of the HVO to have within -- well, certainly the combat forces of the military police, and I believe also other units and anti-terrorists -- what was called an anti-terrorist unit. This was an elite unit. However, there were also other units that were called anti-terrorist units that do not seem to have been part of a specific military battalion. But I don't think I could really provide much more assistance on that. My -- I suppose, to go back to the immediate question, which, if I recall correctly, was to what degree they were independent of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they relied on the logistics of the HVO, from correspondence back and forth. And I know that the Convicts Battalion, in particular, had what appears to be a dedicated sequence of order numbers which was not used by other HVO units but was within the same range. And I suppose the Chamber will be able to see this from the documents before it. I believe it was 02-2/2, or something like this, and then there are numbers above and below that. This indicates that there's at least some degree of integration. But I recognise it's a limited answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry. The documents relating to the independent special units, so-called, were found by you within the HVO archives?

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They also -- there are also other sources of documents, but yes, certainly the ones about which I testified in this particular session, yes, numbers of those were found within the HVO archive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned something which the whole Bench is very interested in, and it was something that you said sort of en personne, that there were some papers that you found within Mr. Naletilic's file. Did you find a Naletilic file within the archive?

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I may have given the wrong impression. I don't recall saying that. I do recall finding papers of or purporting to be of Mr. Naletilic, and there was a file that was called "Units Under the Staff." It was translated in a certain way by the court interpreters. The B/C/S was "Pod Stozerne Postrojbe," and within this set there were a variety of units, a variety -- papers from a variety of units, including those of Mr. Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I see. But there wasn't one specifically on Mr. Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen a file of papers labelled "File of Mr. Naletilic." There were small files, a police file or something like this, but it would be just sort of like an index sheet or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Something like that. Names, I take it, to an historian must be something of vital importance, and I wanted you to explain to us, as somebody of Croatian origin but reared in the United States, of how so many people who come to give evidence in this case or who are referred to in this case and who are adult men have what would appear to us in the West to be babyish nicknames which would have been abandoned once the children went to secondary school. Can you explain the nicknames like "Tuta"?

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I really have no actual experience with that. I do know that nicknames are a popular feature of South Slavic culture, but I don't really know much beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It's got nothing to do with identifying a common surname or anything like that, like one uses in Wales with "Jones" and in Ireland with the name "Ryan"?

utterances.speaker: Marko Prelec [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that does happen, yes. In some places, especially rural areas, one has only a few surnames which are often the same as the village. So to take what may be the best example around here, the very large number of persons named Ahmic from the village of Ahmici. But I don't think that's the only reason why people have nicknames, and those may tend to be somewhat different. I have a friend whose family was from one of these small villages, and there were also just four or five surnames. His entire family had a family nickname which was "Italian," the word "Italian," for obscure reasons, but there are also individual personal nicknames that are adopted by people as they reach adulthood and that may indicate some sort of -- well, you know -- I wouldn't speculate, really. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It's just something, part of the culture, and you can't go beyond that. It's just we've come across it so often we thought maybe you might have been somebody who could help us. Thank you very, very much for your enlightening testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge Clark's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: None, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Thank you, Witness, for giving evidence. You may leave now. Mr. Scott, how about your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Bos will be handling the next witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next witness has requested protective measures, as it was indicated on the list, so he has requested the protective measures of face, voice, and pseudonym. The witness has lived in Mostar and still lives in Mostar, and he feels that he needs this protection in order to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections from the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. After seven days, no, we have no objections. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, as for the facial and the voice distortion, we believe that we need a break for the technicians to have the equipment fixed. We will break for about ten minutes. We will resume at quarter past ten. --- Break taken at 10.05 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I think the witness would have to take the oath first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think you have to brief us with the relevance to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Yes. This witness will testify on the following paragraphs of the indictment: Background, paragraph 10; Superior Authority, paragraph 14; count 1, paragraphs 26 through 30, paragraph 33, paragraph 34(a) and 34(b); counts 2 through 8, paragraphs 35 through 40, and paragraph 44; counts 9 through 12, paragraphs 45 through 48, and paragraph 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, will you please stand up and make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel please come closer to the microphone or switch on his microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, the usher is going to show you a sheet of paper which indicates your name and the pseudonym which you will be testifying under. The Trial Chamber has granted the protective measures, so you'll be testifying under a pseudonym, and your face and your voice will be distorted during your testimony. So could you please have a look at the sheet of paper and tell us -- confirm whether this is -- the name on the paper is, in fact, your name.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, as you could see on the sheet of paper, you'll be referred to as "Witness FF."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: For the first part of my examination, I would like to go into private session, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness FF, could you tell us what happened on the morning of the 9th of May, 1993. Where were you and what happened?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, 1993, sometime around 5.00, the attack on the Vranica building began. That was the building that I lived in. It was 5.00 in the morning, and I was asleep, and so was all my family and all the residents of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What did you do when the attack started?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, the same as everybody else in the building; we all retreated towards the interior part of the building, that is, to the staircase.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you remain there for the rest of the day?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes. All the residents spent the day, the whole of the 9th of May, on the staircase of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you at one moment move somewhere else, into another part of the building, and when was this?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No, I didn't move to another part of the building. The buildings were connected by cellars, but it had been walled up. Only my father and I, and presumably some other people, only went to some flats to get some water and some clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, how long did the attack last?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, the attack lasted for two days. About two days, the 9th and the 10th. That is, in the afternoon of the 10th, the residents of the building surrendered or, rather, stepped out of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you explain what happened when the residents surrendered. Where did you go and what happened?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Since there are joint buildings, there are four entrances. So people went out through their respective entrances. I came out with other people through the front door which belonged to our building, and residents from the adjoining part, because that part was on fire, they moved through the cellar where the wall was broken down. They reached our front door and came out into the yard of the building together with us. Another group of people whose front door was on the other side of the building, they came out into the west part of the yard, whereas we had come out into the east part of the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, is it correct that you made a drawing of the building and what you just explained? Did you put that in a drawing?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness this drawing which the witness made, and I have copies for Your Honours as well. It will be marked as Exhibit P884, and the Defence was provided with a copy just before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we be informed, when was this drawing made?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This drawing was made on this Monday, when I spoke with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I wonder if this drawing could be put on the ELMO so the witness could make some indications.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this drawing?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you explain what you have written down. First of all, which is -- which of the squares is the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: This here is the Vranica building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. And then you've drawn a square on the left with the letter "E." What does that represent?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: This is the School of Economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: There appears to be a road running along these two complexes which you have indicated as "SR." What did that represent?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: That's the Stjepana Radica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, could you please explain what happened on the 10th of May; where you actually exited the building and where other tenants of that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. building exited. And you've made some drawings. Could you please explain this in detail.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: The tenants who lived in this part of the building, that part of the building caught fire, and these people, through the basement, managed to arrive in our part of the building which had been shelled but was not on fire. And together with us, they exited this way, whereas the tenants who were here, at the very corner, exited here in front of the School of Economics. Also, there was a fourth entrance, and the people living there exited as shown with the arrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, could you please repeat which exit you took on the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I exited here, using this entrance. In fact, that is -- that is the -- that was the entrance to my section of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: For the record, this is the exit which is on the right side of the square, the middle arrow, pointing outside the square. Could the witness now be shown Exhibit 11.13, please. Yes. This exhibit could be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: [redacted]. That's the Vranica building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could we put Exhibit P884 again on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you please indicate with the pointer which side of the building is, in fact, depicted on that photograph. Where on the drawing would that side of the building be?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: It would be this side, the west side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The left side of the square. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes, the left side on the sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, there are three more squares which we haven't discussed. One is the square just above the square which depicts -- which is the Vranica building, and it's a square which is indicated with a "P," a big square with a "P." What is this building?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: That was the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And were any of the tenants who were taken out of the building, were they taken to that building, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: All the tenants were taken to that building except for me and another smaller group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how many people are we talking about who were taken to this police station?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, these were the tenants from two entrances. So it could have been 300 people, 200 to 300 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You testified that you were taken somewhere else. Where were you taken or where did you go?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I went with a smaller group to the hospital, which we called surgery, and we carried the wounded there. It is the one marked with the letter "H" on the drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you said you carried the wounded. How many wounded people were there?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: We carried four wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And could you tell me who they were and what type of injuries they had? You don't have to call their names but what type of persons they were.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: There were two ABiH members. One was wounded in the back, and I believe the other had a stomach injury. There were a young girl of age 10 who had a head injury, and there was a man of an advanced age who was wounded in both legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were these people wounded by bullet wounds, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I assumed that they were bullet wounds, but I cannot be 100 per cent sure. It was either shrapnel or bullet wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What happened after you had delivered these wounded people at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: This group in which I was, we were about ten altogether, and we were taken to -- immediately to this other police station which was next door to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was this police station also referred to by another name, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes. She is much better known as "the stone building."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What happened to you when you arrived at the stone building?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: They took us to the inner courtyard of this police station, and they placed us in two small rooms which had metal doors, and they were without windows, very small rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, who is "they"? Who took you there?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how did you recognise these people as members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms. And because there was an attack, they had the tricolour ribbons - the tricolour was the Croatian tricolour - on their shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: For how long did you stay at this police station called the stone building?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I stayed three days and three nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you ever interrogated in this building?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes, on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who interrogated you on the first occasion?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I was interrogated by a person whose last name was Bosnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what did he ask you?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: He asked me whether I was a member of the army, what I was doing. The standard questions; why I was shooting at Croats and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you beaten on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what about the second time you were interrogated; by whom were you interrogated on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I was interrogated on that occasion by two members in uniforms without any insignia. This was in the stone building, so I assumed that they were members of the Herceg-Bosna MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you explain what happened during this second interrogation. Did anything particular happen?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: At the very beginning, when I entered the room, I saw that the window was open. And the very beginning, they told me, "Try to escape. Your colleague before tried to and did not succeed."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I sat down in the chair. I did not try anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you later find out who this colleague was, as they referred to? Did you speak with that man afterwards?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Later on we met at Ljubuski, also in the camp. He used to be a judge before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What did he tell you what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: He told me that he was, in fact, pushed out that window, and this was the height of about 5 to 6 metres. And he fell in front of the main entrance to the building and twisted or broke his ankle. And then a guard shot him in his legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, where were you taken after your detention at this local police station?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: The whole group was moved to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how long were you detained for in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: About one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: During your detention in the Ljubuski prison, was this prison ever visited by a man named Romeo Blazevic and another man named Ernest Takac?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes, both of them came two days after our arrival at Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know for which unit these two people were serving?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: They said that they were members of the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you know these people from before the war, or was this the first time you met them?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I used to know them by sight from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You said that they arrived on the second day of your detention. What did they do on that -- at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: They came on the second day, and they were looking for an ABiH member who was an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what was the name of that person who they were looking for?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: That was Rudolf Jozelic, J-O-Z-E-L-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did they find this man in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes, he was in the cell with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What did they do to this man?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: They beat him up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you witness this beating?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No. But after a while, we were all brought out into the courtyard, and we saw him covered in blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did this man, Rudolf Jozelic, later on tell you what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: He told me that they had beaten him with a shovel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Where had they beaten him?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: All over his body. They broke several of his ribs and nose.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you said that you and the other prisoners were taken out, and that's when you saw Rudolf Jozelic. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: After that, they also hit several times, they kicked and punched two journalists several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who is "they," when you refer to "they"?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: These were two journalists who were journalists before the war, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. one who was called Alija Lizde, L-I-Z-D-E, and the other one Dzemal Hamzic, H-A-M-Z-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: By whom were they beaten?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: By both of them. That means both by Takac and by Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did -- after this beating, did Takac talk to you?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes. He asked me for my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you give your name?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes, I told him my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What did he then ask you, or then what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: In fact, he recognised my name. Did he not know me, but he knew my father. And after that, he asked me whether I knew the Jukic brothers, J-U-K-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How did you respond?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I responded that I did know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what did he tell you then?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: He told me they came here to beat the balijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was he then referring to the Jukic brothers or was he referring to himself?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: He was referring to them, to the Jukic brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you beaten on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, was there ever a time when a man arrived at the Ljubuski prison by the name of -- who identified himself as the brother of Cikota?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What happened when he arrived? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: He also came looking for members of the army, but like people before him and after him, he was -- he also was looking for Rudi Jozelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you know what he did to Rudi Jozelic when he found him?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: He also beat him up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I object to the form of that question. It assumes facts not in evidence, and it's also leading and suggestive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the question is: "What happened when he arrived? What did he do? What do you know, and do you know what he did?" Well, I don't think it's a leading question. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Jozelic was also -- was beaten up. Did you witness this beating?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How do you know then that he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Later, he was taken to the hospital to bandage his ribs, because again he suffered fractured ribs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was there ever a time that a man by the name of Tuta visited Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you tell me approximately when that was and what he did.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Perhaps ten days after my arrival at Ljubuski, a group of prisoners was brought from Siroki Brijeg. They told me that they had been at Tuta's prison, that they had worked for him on some construction at some swimming pool. And Mr. Tuta came the following day for them, because apparently they had been brought to Ljubuski without his knowledge, and he needed them to finish the work that they were doing for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're saying that he came to collect prisoners? Did he in fact take prisoners on that day with him?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, did you see this man by the name of Tuta on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How did you know that he visited Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: He only took younger prisoners, those who could work, and the older ones were left behind, and it was they who told me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You said that you stayed for about a month in Ljubuski. Where were you taken after Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: After Ljubuski, I was taken to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know approximately what date that was?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I think it was the first week of the month of June. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, while being in the Heliodrom, were you ever being interrogated?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Only -- on one day only, they took our personal data, that is, the full names and dates of birth. There was no real interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you were taken out of -- that you were taken to an office by somebody while being detained in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: That was perhaps seven to ten days after I was brought to the Heliodrom. They called me out, and I followed the guard to a nearby small building, which was about 10 to 20 metres away from the central prison building at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to ask to go into private session for the next couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we are approaching the break. Can you finish your questioning in 3 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Then I would prefer that we continue after the break, if that's acceptable. Because it will take a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the break, I asked if we could go into private session. I don't know if we can do that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I was at the Heliodrom until the 1st of July. On the 30th of June, 1st of July, some 20, 22 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And where were you taken on the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: We were taken to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you know why you were taken to Dretelj? Why couldn't you stay at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: They relocated us to Dretelj because a large number of Bosniak prisoners were about to arrive. On the 30th of June, the Armija Bosnia-Herzegovina liberated a part of the territory, and then HVO men were rounding up all men, all Bosniak men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: For how long did you stay at the Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Twenty days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How were the conditions in the Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: It was the worst camp of all that I had been in. The conditions were there as in Auschwitz in World War II or some such concentration camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you ever witness any beatings while you were in Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: On two occasions; once I saw the beating. The second time, I only heard it, because those men had been taken out of the hangar in which we were kept. On that first occasion, HVO men burst in, and they mostly beat elderly men, using batons and fists and feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: The second time, we could only hear the blows and the cries of pain. And after that, we saw people swollen with bruises, and there was blood on some of them, but we could not see what they had been beaten with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the Dretelj camp was?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I did not see him ever, but I heard the mention of a name Anicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who guarded the Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: For how long did you stay in the Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: About 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And where were you taken after your detention at the Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: After Dretelj, they took us back to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: While you were back at the Heliodrom, were you ever taken out for labour?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Not during the first ten days because we were all very weak. After that, they took us to the separation line, to the front line, in Mostar, that is, Bulevar and Santiceva Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: On how many occasions were you taken -- on how many occasions were you taken to the Santiceva Street?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Four, five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what was the type of work that you had to do there?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Mostly repairing trenches and bunkers, filling the bags and carrying the bags to the front line. I mean sandbags, sandbags for the bunkers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who guarded you?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: There were guards who were members of the 2nd Battalion of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You testified earlier that you also worked at the Bulevar. How many times did you work at the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I was there only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And that one occasion that you were taken to the Bulevar, who took you there?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Guards and the driver arrived. I didn't know them, and they put 12 of us into a van, and then took us to Rondo, to a house there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of that house or the person who lived in that house?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: It was Peskina Street. That was the last name of the family which used to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you please spell that name for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: P-E-S-K-E [sic], Peske [sic]. That was the family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people who you saw there when you were taken to this house of Dr. Peskina?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes. I knew some of the men before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Where did you know them from?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I knew them by sight, because they were from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you find out for which unit these people were working?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: They were under the command of Benito Sesar, but they all talked about being Stela's ATG.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you referred to "Stela's ATG." Have you ever met this person called Stela?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, where did the soldiers take you when you were guarded in this house of Peskina?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: They took us to a house which we all knew as Dr. Aleksic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what did you have to do there?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: There we had to repair the trenches and the bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And while you were doing this work, was there any fighting going on at that moment?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes. A couple of times fire was opened against the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did there come a time in August that you were again taken to work at Santiceva Street?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know which date that was?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I remember the date when I was wounded. It was the 30th of August. I was taken to the Santiceva Street, or more precisely, to the old post office in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, you said that you got wounded. Could you please explain what kind of work you had to do and how you got wounded.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: It was a group of five prisoners. We were brought to a residential building which was at the front line, and we were taken to the mezzanine level to reinforce that line. It was a door to the balcony that was used as a parapet, and they wanted it filled up with sandbags up to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the ceiling, and our task was to do that at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how did you get wounded?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: At the moment when I went to pick up a bag, I heard a shot and a bullet passed through both my arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you see where the bullet came from?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I saw with the corner of my eye sort of a flame from the rifle that had fired. It was to my left, the side where the other prisoners were and the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So who do you think -- who do you think shot -- made that shot? Who shot at you, do you think?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I believe that it was a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What kind of injury did you get to your arm?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I had both arms fractured. All my nerves were blown. And this was an explosive type of round, one that exploded when it hit you. So my muscle was blown. And they had to take a muscle from the back and implant it, and also I had my arm put in a fixator.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did the wound heal? Is your arm functioning again?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: The doctors did what they could. They couldn't do more. So it healed as much as it could have. I now have about 10 percent of the use of the arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. I am the attorney of the accused Naletilic, and I will ask you certain questions. I am going to be asking questions, and I am going to endeavour to frame them in such a way as to get the shortest possible answer from them. So will you please listen to me very carefully as I ask them, and I also will have to turn off my microphone before you answer. Witness, will you tell me, at whose request did you make the drawing that is still on the monitor here?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: At my own request so that I could explain things better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: To explain better what?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: The paths that the tenants used to exit the building, and also its relation to other buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And why did you think that important?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: In order to be understood which side each group -- by which side each group left the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the statement that you gave to the AID in 1995?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you recall the statement that you gave to the investigators of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you recall that in both of these statements that you were taken in front of the stone building?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you ever mention the tenants in any of your statements?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, of course, when we get there, I will give you the statements that you've given to review, and I have enough copies. But in your first statement, you never mentioned any tenants, and in the second, just briefly that you were separated from them. But two days before your evidence, suddenly you felt the urge and then even produce a drawing to talk about all the tenants. This is only two days before you were to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me give you a map of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Prosecution Exhibit -- This is a Prosecution Exhibit, Number P11.18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do we have Defence counsel's number for that? I mean a D number. Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Well, I've just provided the witness with the official copy of the exhibit, so it's P11.18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, will you please take the pointer, and will you please show me on this map here where the stone building was.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is that near the Splitska Street?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please talk into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The witness has been shown an exhibit with other markings on it, and I don't think that's very appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I've already noted that. And Madam Registrar will produce a clean one.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: It is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We can say that this is in the street between the Stjepana Radica and Splitska Streets.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, can you tell me where the hospital is where you took the wounded persons?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: At the corner, right by the stone building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: At this very corner of Kralj Tvrtko Street and the street where the stone building was?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please put number "1" there. Or perhaps we can place letter "H," which is an international sign for hospital.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And above it, will you please mark with "P" where the police station was.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Can you tell me now -- now we can see on the map, and we can see what route you took. The 13 of you were then taken to the stone building to be interrogated.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You don't know what happened to the others from the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: You mean the other tenants?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you don't know what happened to the soldiers either?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No, except I know that they passed by the fence of this first police station building and they entered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who was that; the residents? the tenants?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Will you now tell me, Witness, do you have any knowledge about any of the units which, as you said, had attacked the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Who took part -- I don't know which units took part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You see, Witness, in the statement you gave on 8 January 1995 [sic], I believe it was -- no. Sorry, it was 1996. I have a pretty illegible copy. So that was the 6th of January 1996 when your recollection was at its freshest. Apart from being taken in front of the stone building, there's no mention of any carrying of the wounded, and today in your evidence, what you testified to today, you never mention it. You never mention events in Ljubuski in which Takac was involved. There is not even a "T" of Tuta in it. There's nothing about the Heliodrom. And you gave that statement two years after all these events had happened to you. The statement that you gave to the investigators of this Tribunal, it seems as -- on the 5th of October, 1998, it seems as if your recollection came back. Now we have names. Mladen Naletilic appears in it. Tell me, did they ask you about those names, the investigators?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: What investigators are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The investigators of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: They did not ask me anything about them. I just said what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And why did you not say that to the investigators of the secret police?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: First because I was not sure I wanted to give testimony, and then there were a lot of people there so I didn't feel that it was confidential enough for me to give such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask the usher. I have nine copies in English. I believe that my learned friends from the Prosecution have it, and I have one copy in B/C/S for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Which statement is the witness going to see now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement given to the AID on the 6th of January, 1996, my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, will you be so kind to read to yourself the first statement that you gave to the organs of - how shall I put it? - your own entity, the secret police, which is also known as AID. And please find me any of the names Romeo Blazevic, Takac, Tuta, any mention of the wounded. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. You were telling the truth when you were testifying, and you told the whole truth?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I did not tell any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, what details were omitted? Did you consider them insignificant when you omitted them?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I did consider them important, but I wasn't -- I didn't feel safe. There were too many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: There were too many people?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I was just wondering, could my learned colleague please pay attention to the microphone, because he keeps the microphone on, and he should make an effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, my learned friend. I will pay attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So my question was: How do you mean too many people? These were the organs of your police. How many people were present there when you were questioned?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: There were three, but non-stop people were going in and out, and two or three witnesses were giving evidence at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, this is referring to the same case?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Different cases, but the general information was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So how could the investigators of this Tribunal come and talk to you when in the statement that you gave to the AID -- and we know that the AID has been closely cooperating with this institution, how did they arrive at you? How did it come about that you came to testify before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: The same as I was called for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who called you for the first time?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness, members of the police or members of the secret police?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Members of the AID.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So the second time that they appeared, they told you what, exactly?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The second time when they came to you, were they present when you gave your evidence to the investigators of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But they took you to the location where the investigators of this Tribunal were waiting for you?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you then tell me, they had the statement that you had given to the AID?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Probably they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So what questions did they ask of you?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: The normal ones. I don't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness, in your first statement, there is nothing that has anything to do with this case, the evidence of today. Maybe it has something to do with some other cases. And they had the statement you had given to the AID, and they see that there's nothing that relates to this case because there's no name. There's just some general things that happened to you. How did you arrive at Romeo Blazevic, Ernest Takac, the Convicts Battalion, Cikota? How did you arrive at that?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: That is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, how did you know that Romeo Blazevic and Ernest Takac were members of the Convicts Battalion? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: This is what people were saying. That's what I said, that people were saying that they were members of the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You only know about it from what people were saying?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And then that story you considered important enough to tell the investigators?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: What was important was what they did, not whose members they were or members of what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I agree with what you're saying. But now you are assuming a position of an experienced lawyer. Did anyone before this testimony ever show you the photographs of these men?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you who these men were while questioning you?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: How could they if they didn't even show me the photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, on that occasion, you told the investigators, "I recognise Tuta by the photographs." And you used plural, the photographs that you saw.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: That is some kind of a mistake. There was only one photograph extant. It may be a typo or some kind of omission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How did you know that the man whom you named Cikota was, indeed, Cikota?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: The guards told us that it was Cikota's brother, and he was wearing a black ribbon of mourning. And Cikota had been killed prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So this was not Cikota, then; it was Cikota's brother?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: It was always Cikota's brother. This could be some kind of mistake in translation. I never said that this was Cikota.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So the guards told you this?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And this man, was he a policeman, a civilian? What was he?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Which man?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Cikota's brother.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I don't know. He had uniform and a black -- actually, no, it was a black badge, a pin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you also heard from other people that his brother had been killed?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: This is what people were saying around town, that Cikota was killed somewhere around Jablanica even before the conflict in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This is what people were talking about in town -- you mean in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean in coffee bars, the same coffee bars where you also saw Mr. Naletilic's photograph?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The photograph that you supposedly saw in a coffee bar, a photograph of Mr. Naletilic, was that a small photograph? Where was it in --

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: It was on the wall behind the bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And do you know the name of that coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: It was right next to the municipal stadium. It was called Zerenski.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And will you please describe to this Trial Chamber how Mr. Bosnjic looked.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Blond, short hair, average height, shorter than I, not too well-built, but it was -- he was built well enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, will you take me as an example. Was he taller or shorter than I?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: He was about your height.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I am 173 metres [sic] tall, for the record. And he was well-built?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes. He wasn't really built up, but he was strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear in town that Mr. Bosnjic lost half of his head by a sniper bullet on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And he was over 190 tall?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No. I did not say that that was him. I just said what the prisoners told me based on my description who it could have been. I never said that that was the man, because I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You stated that. You said clearly, "That was his bodyguard Bosnjic." Now we hear that you had heard that from others.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: It was always that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please look at the statement that you have in front of you, the second statement before the investigators of this Tribunal, not the AID. Will you turn to page 2 of that statement. The last paragraph, third line. "There was his bodyguard Bosnjic." You said that expressly. Do you have the same statement as I do? So this was a statement to the investigators of the Tribunal. Bottom of the second page, last passage, or, rather, it says -- no. It says "3." Third page, last passage.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, on my copy it is on the fourth page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know why is it on page 4. Perhaps you have a page more than I do, and that wouldn't surprise me either. Have you found it where it says that?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So, "There was his bodyguard Bosnjic." And you still affirm that he was a bodyguard? And that he was a bodyguard, you had that too?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, I said the same thing then as I'm saying now. I don't know why is this. And I just said I described the man, because it was the first time I had seen him. So I described him to some other prisoners, and they told me that he was his bodyguard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness FF, are you -- do you know what you are saying? Do you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. realise the horror when you say something that you do not know and you claim here that you do? Because it was on the basis of this statement that the indictment -- that charges were brought. And you claim here that it was his bodyguard Bosnjic.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: When I gave that statement, that is not what I said. I said that other prisoners had told me -- having heard my description of the man, they told me that he was his bodyguard and that that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But it does not say so in your statement, nor was your testimony today such.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You said the name quite explicitly, that he was a bodyguard, and when my learned friend asked you, you then came up with a broader explanation. Can we therefore conclude that you have no idea who that man was, if he ever struck you, that is?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I've been saying from the very beginning that it was from other prisoners who told me that it could be he said so. I never affirmed that it was he.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Oh, very well. Can you then explain how is it that you know -- how is it that you knew that Mr. Naletilic was building a restaurant, that he needed prisoners to build it?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: The prisoners themselves told me so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Prisoners from which prison or camp or detention centre?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Those who joined us in Ljubuski and who had come from Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, did Tuta ever visit Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I did not see him, but prisoners who did see him said that, yes, he visited there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know that no other witness said that apart from you, and they also were in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard your comment, my learned friend, but there is this incident in the coffee bar but not the prison. I know all the statements -- I know the statements by heart, my learned friend. I'm talking about the Ljubuski prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you heard that too, that other people saw him. And you also heard that he was building a pool. Today you said you heard it from some relatively young people. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I didn't say it was young people who had told me. I said that he took younger prisoners to build that restaurant, that pool.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: What do you mean "when"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: At what period of time?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: When he was in Ljubuski you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Those younger prisoners who told you that.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Those prisoners that you call younger persons, when did they tell you that they worked there?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: When they came to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And then they stayed with you. They did not go anywhere again?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No, no, no. They came the first day to Ljubuski and then they told us where they had come from. And they -- later, most of them went back to Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So most of them went back to Siroki Brijeg, and they returned and --

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: And I don't know what happened to them. They went back to Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
