utterances.text: I have some difficulties here, Mr. Krsnik. Could I offer some advice to the witness. Witness, since you and the Defence counsel are speaking the same language, please wait until the question. And you see in the mike this is a red line. When you see the Defence counsel turn off that red line, you begin to answer the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You see this red light here?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, then, pay attention. Until I switch this off, then don't speak. It is for your own safety, as we speak the same language and so we forget ourselves. Tell me, please, in your statement, you explicitly say, "The Convicts Battalion did not harm me in any way." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I mean the beating. None of the members of the Convicts Battalion beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And how do you know who is a member of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Some of them I knew by sight, but they could mostly enter without any passes or anything. I mean enter the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So those who enter the prison without a pass, it was your conclusion, then, that those were men from the Convicts Battalion. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And whom -- who is it that you knew by sight? Tell us. We don't need a private session. Which members did you know by sight from before who came to Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, I know those two that I already mentioned, Romeo and Takac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But a while ago we concluded that you did not know that; it was merely your inference.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying the same thing, that I knew them by sight and by what I had heard from others, that they were members of the Convicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My dear witness, I deeply sympathize with you and all that befell you, believe me. But this is a very serious examination. So will you please, when you say "I know," not to say "I know" but to say "I heard." Because when you say "I know," it means "I heard." Yet, you do not know; you only heard it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this. He says that -- he has testified that he knew that he had seen these persons before in Mostar. That's what he testified. He didn't know the names, but he had seen these persons before. That's what he knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we have to take whatever the witness’s answer to the question is. If he said he knows that, we have to take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is very difficult here to conduct the procedure. We're all criminal lawyers, and the witnesses for the Prosecution who are offered to us, we can only conduct our cross-examination on the basis of the Criminal Code and the Criminal Procedure Act. We have read those statements, and we know what it's all about, but we have to show it and prove it to this Court. And the Prosecution could have been of help to us, and then all these things wouldn't have happened, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we understand where you are leading us to, but you don't need to send a warning signal to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, excuse me. With your leave, I hope you understood me. I merely wanted to warn the witness that giving testimony is a serious matter, and I wanted to remind him of the circumstances under which all this happened because I could see that the witness was very well led until my cross-examination. So I merely wanted to explain it. But thank you very much for the warning. I shall try to bring these things to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And let us finish all this grapevine thing. That is, tourists in the prison or in Mostar, one man says something to another one and then he says it was somebody to a third person, and then it reaches your ears. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, whether it's the fifth or the sixth. But yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, distinguished witness, this chief of the military police, Josip Marcinko, you called him the chief of the military police, didn't you? And is that something that you know or is it something that you heard again?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Oh, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was he the chief of the military police at the Heliodrom or of the city or?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: He was the chief of the military police. He was the chief of the military police of the city, not the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What was he doing at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I don't know. He was in Tuta's company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And which guards were there at the Heliodrom? Who guarded the Heliodrom? Who guarded it?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Members of the military police, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Why do you say, "I guess"? Didn't you see white belts? I see that you can see all sorts of things, but you don't see who's guarding you.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, they wore different things. They didn't have all identical uniforms, nor did they all have white belts. Some of them had brown belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But did they have military police badges?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: At times. Well, no, it varied from one man to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness FF, I'll show you a photograph now. It is Prosecutor's Exhibit 20.2. I will then ask you to show you something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the usher please help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness FF, will you please take the pointer. Now, I will ask you first to -- for one, sir, establish where was the prison and where were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the other buildings? Which building served as the prison? Would you be so kind as to point at them.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I can't see very well because there are those trees here. The first time I was in prison, I never left the central prison, that is, the building called that. So I'm not sure of that facility. I never saw it from the outside except that particular moment, but only glimpsed it because I was outside for only a couple of moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how many buildings there were? We are talking about the Heliodrom, about a huge thing, but here there are heaps of buildings. Do you know how many constituted the prison, one or two, or if you want, the camp which is called the Heliodrom here?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, it was comprised of this building that was called the central prison, then the school building, because the Heliodrom used to be the secondary air school -- air navigation school, and the gymnasium, so the -- the basketball hall rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So these are the three buildings; the central one, the school, and the basketball hall. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So how about other buildings, because all this is called the Heliodrom, isn't it? So who was in those other buildings?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: The military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell me, please, was -- were those three buildings fenced off? Was there a fence around them? Did they have guards?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: There was no fence around the buildings. There was an outside fence. It was fenced around on the outside, around the -- its outside perimeter because it was a military school. It was a military school, and there were guards at the entrance of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So each one of those buildings had a guard at the entrance, I mean those facilities that you called a prison, and the whole Heliodrom was surrounded by fence and had its own guards. Do I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: The whole camp had a fence around it, and I think it was only the main gate that they had their guards. But each one of the buildings had its own guard at the front door.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who guarded it, that is, the Heliodrom as such and each of these buildings individually?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, the military police, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, will you please be so kind, Witness FF, to point at the building in which Tuta interrogated you. I mean, this thing that you told us today about.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, I can't really find my way around this, because I'm not sure which one is the central building. I'm not really sure. I think that this is the central building, this one here, and right next to it was this small house. But I cannot really affirm that with certainty, because I never had the opportunity to walk around the compound and thus identify every building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, what small house was it? Or let me try to help you. Was it an independent house? How big was it; 150 square metres, one room, two rooms?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: There were several rooms in it, but I was in only one of them which served as an office, and it could have been about 15, 20 square metres large, 4 by 4 perhaps, and it is a one-storey building, but there were, nevertheless, stairs leading into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And apart from Mr. Marcinko, was there anyone else present there?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: There was this military policeman, the guard who had escorted me there into that office, and he was present there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Oh, I see. See this house has nothing to do with the prison. It's outside those three buildings, is it?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now tell me, please, which was the purpose of this interrogation? I mean I listened carefully to what was said. And he inquired about your father. I don't understand really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik. Well, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I would like to go into private session if we're going to discuss this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am being very careful, Your Honour, and I know what I asked. For the time being, there is absolutely no risk here. A question about "your father" does not mean anything, and I am really mindful of the way I ask my questions. But if you insist, of course we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since the direct examination was conducted in the private session, in the cross-examination, we should do so, go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In your first statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In your first session, you mentioned mostly Ljubinje. These were the positions 50 kilometres away from Mostar, on the front line facing the Chetniks. In your second statement, you mention only the Santic Street, and there you have a sentence, "When I worked there, I never saw anyone from the Convicts Battalion." Now, I ask you once again: Had you even -- if you had seen them, how would you know that they came from the Convicts Battalion? First you said these people were from the Convicts Battalion. Now you tell us, "When I worked there, I did not see anybody from the Convicts Battalion."

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I said the same thing on both occasions. Ljubinje is mentioned in deference -- with reference to the time when I was in Ljubuski, and that is when we were taken to work on the front lines facing the Serb troops, when you set off towards Svetava. And the second time, I said it was on Santic Street that I did see anyone from the Convicts Battalion, except on one occasion when I worked in Dr. Aleksic's house on Bulevar where this ATG was, where there was the Benito Sesar, the commander about whom we knew, that he was a member of the Convicts Battalion. It was an independent unit, making part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This is the first time you are mentioning this. You did not say that in your first or your second statement. Tell me, and what was this Benito Sesar's unit called?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Oh, I don't know that. It was ATG, but exact name ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And then you again make your conjectures, again the story goes round, and you hear that Benito Sesar and his ATG are part of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, they were all connected. Everybody knew that he was -- he had to do with both Stela and Tuta.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who said "everybody else"?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, that was common knowledge. They were members of the same unit even before the conflict with the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And that is another thing that you heard, or is it something that you know?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Well, they were non-stop together. They went into actions together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who did?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Those members whom I knew. They were together in operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, were you ever in those actions with them?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were you ever present when they went off into action?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know which actions?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No. In the area of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know how many; one unit, or is it the HVO, or ...

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: They were a unit of its own. Everybody called it the Convicts Battalion, members of the Convicts Battalion. Many of them bragged about being members of the Convicts Battalion. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Ha. Now we are coming to an interesting question. Those who bragged about it. Did many people brag about that? "I'm Tuta's boy, Stela's boy." Were there many such? Because every unit had its commander, and every -- and commanders identified themselves with them and that is how they called themselves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, those who boasted, were there many such?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Not too many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But you know Mostar. You grew up there. You know people there, don't you? Can one believe one who brags around in Mostar? You -- don't you check that?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No. But the whole city spoke about those who were members of the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see that we're coming to the lunch break. I shall be very, very brief after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume at 2.30 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, in the statement that you gave to the investigators of this Tribunal, on page 3 in my version, probably page 4 in yours, you said that the beating of prisoners was in places where the other prisoners could not see it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: What is this in reference to? I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I thought that you did. The usher will assist you. This is in reference to the prison in Ljubuski. In my text, it's page 3. In yours, it's probably page 4. This is the statement you gave to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No, I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In addition to the fact that you didn't see it, you also said that others could also not see it.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It's on page 3 or 4. It's the paragraph one. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, now, in addition to the fact that you couldn't see it, which is what you stated, this is the second sentence: "The beatings of prisoners was usually carried out in places where the other prisoners could not see."

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes. Only those who were beaten were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So the rest you could only learn from people talking about it?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes, from the prisoners who had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But you only mentioned four prisoners who could have personally witnessed the condition of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So not everybody could come in contact with them.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: These were the prisoners from my cell who had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, will you please read the paragraph. You said something completely different. You said that the persons who could see that were those four prisoners, and you did not say that they were beaten.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I'm talking -- Jozelic was with me in the cell, and he had been beaten, and the others saw him afterwards and saw his condition afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you tell me how many cells, how many buildings this Ljubuski prison has? How big was it and where was it?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: We arrived late at night in that prison in Ljubuski, so I did not see exactly where the prison was located. I only know that it was near a local stadium, maybe a few hundred metres from a stadium. Maybe it wasn't a local stadium. Maybe it was just a sports field or something. And the prison was not large. It consisted of one house, a building, one could say. It was a good-sized building. And the cells were rooms in -- on the ground floor, very small in size. My cell measured perhaps 2 by 3.5 metres, so 7 or 8 square metres in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did this building have some kind of an inner courtyard?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the windows of the rooms in which you were staying, were they looking out onto the courtyard or the street?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Those cells did not have windows looking out on the street, and there were -- I know that there were some windows overlooking the backyard, but there may have also been some windows overlooking the street, but that would be in the rooms where the soldiers were staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were you able to look out through the window?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I was not in a room which had windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, tell me, were you a member of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, why did you not mention that anywhere until today? You always stated that you were a civilian.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: That is not correct. I always stated that I was a member of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to wait for you, but will you please find a place where you say that in these two statements.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Where shall I find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You cannot find it because you never said it anywhere. On the contrary, you said on page 1 of the statement you gave to the investigators, on the third paragraph, in the middle, you said: "I was a civilian, and one of my neighbours told him that." This is in reference to your interrogation in the stone building. Did you find that? Go ahead. Read it, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes, I did find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you see that here you claim that you were a civilian.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: This was wrongly translated, and it was taken out of the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you clarify that a bit? How do you -- how is it taken out of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. context if one says that one is a member of ABiH and then it comes that it -- then it appears in the statement that one is a civilian?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I said it in order to fare easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think this question and answer is to be redacted. You may proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then move into private session, please, just in case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to a private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness FF. I am Zelimir Par; I am one of the Defence attorneys for Vinko Martinovic. I will ask you several questions, but I would like to take you first to the incident in Ljubuski. You mentioned two soldiers, Romeo Blazevic and Ernest Takac. Can you tell me whether you personally saw their arrival in the prison in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You did not see them. Did you see them at all on that occasion, during that incident, personally?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: What incident? The beating of Jozelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So all this is secondhand, from what others said, that is, from the source that you heard, from Jozelic and others; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes, from what Jozelic said. And I saw them punching and kicking those two journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did Jozelic tell this to you personally, or did he tell this to other people and you heard it from them?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: He told everyone who was in the cell, where we were all locked up together. He didn't talk to anyone in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what time of day or night was it when this took place?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: That was late in the afternoon, perhaps early evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: On that occasion, did Jozelic say that they came as part of a unit, or did they come on their own, sort of ...

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought that you said -- that you had asked me when this happened. This happened in the late afternoon, and he told us later that night what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, that is what I understood you to have said. But when he told you about it, did he tell you whether Blazevic and Takac came as part of a unit that arrived at around that time, or did they come on their own, out of control?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: He did not know himself how they got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did he perhaps say whether they were inebriated or on drugs, or could he observe anything like that?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: He did not mention anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was in charge of you, the prisoners, that is? Who was guarding you there? Was it police? Was it army?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I assume that that was the military police from Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation of how those two men could enter past that military police guard? Were they members of the military police or how could they have entered bypassing the military police?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Prlic, who was their commander, who was a commander of the Ljubuski prison, said that he could stop individual members of the HVO who were coming in to beat soldiers but that he could not stop others from coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether Jozelic complained to anyone, to any of the commanders to what had happened to him, that he had been attacked, that he had been beaten up? Did he ever complain? Did he ever tell any of the command structure what had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: You mean in the prison? There was nothing they could do. They were not in a position to help him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And do you know whether any of the commanders, that is, superiors of Blazevic or Takac, ever learned about this incident ever?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I'm in no position to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let me now take you forward to the Bulevar and the period when you were sent from the Heliodrom to work. Did you -- have you ever heard about a unit called Vinko Skrobo?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know what part of the front line was held by that unit?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I heard that they held an area around Krankasa, that is, around the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a map, and I'm going to ask you to try to orient yourself there and show us where that unit was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the registry for map P12.1 and have it placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: First, can you please study the map a little bit so that you can orient yourself and then we'll place it on the ELMO, and I'm going to ask you to mark -- to show the place which you just mentioned where that unit had its zone of responsibility or where they held their positions.

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: It would be the area here. Approximately where mark "1" is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes. That is mark "1." Can you now, in the caption on the top left corner, can you read what it says?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes. That is Krankasa, or that is also known as the health centre or the infirmary popularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes. Then you said that you were brought to the Rondo and that the person who was in charge of you was a certain Benito Sesar. The question is: Do you know to which unit you were brought there?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: It was also an ATG, but I don't know the name of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the Benko Penavic ATG?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and that was the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know where this Benko Penavic had its zone of responsibility, and if you do, could you please show us on this map?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I was with them. I was at their line, section of line. So that is immediately adjacent to the Krankasa but on the other side of the street. I can't use my arm very well. Oh, yes. Here it is. It is Dr. Aleksic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly that you just answered me that on that occasion you worked for the Benko Penavic ATG at Aleksic's house?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, if we can just look at another thing on the map. You said that you were -- that you disembarked at the Rondo. This is where Benito Sesar waited for you. Can you please show the Rondo, where it was that Rondo?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: I can't see it well, but is this number 6 there?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes. Can you see on -- in the -- what it says in the top left corner what number 6 stands for?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: That is headquarters of the Benko Penavic ATG.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: This location was also known as Peske's house. So that was the Peskes' house that you mentioned as the place that you were. Thank you, Witness FF.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Just maybe just to -- I would like to tender Exhibit P884, which is the drawing made by Witness FF.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This map -- yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I would like to enter the map that we showed the witness. That would be P12.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But, Mr. Krsnik, do you have any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour, but I thought that we would wait. Usually we've been waiting for the end of the examination, but of course I would like to tender Prosecution P11.18. This is our exhibit D1/30. And the previous statements of this witness in their entirety. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The map proposed by the Prosecutor with the number P884 has been admitted into evidence. Any objections to the Defence counsels' tendering of the documents? Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: With regard to the previous statements of the witness, we have the same objection as we stated before, that we don't consider this as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about the other exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: On the other exhibit, there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, pending the decisions made by this Trial Chamber concerning the previous statements, at this moment, Madam Registrar will give them an ID number so that we can know where these documents will be located. As for that document D1/30, it has been admitted into evidence. Judge Diarra has a question to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, at the time of your arrest at your building, was your place searched? I mean, at the time when you came out of the building and surrendered, were you searched then?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: In the beginning, I don't know. I don't think anybody did that while we were still there, but whilst we were still in the building, I do not think anybody would dare because of the very fierce fire there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you came out of the building when the fire stopped, is that it?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: We came out with a white flag in the afternoon the next day, and then we were taken over by HVO men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You spoke about labour duty on the front line. Was the work that you were engaged in dangerous?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes, because it was on the front line itself, and we were in the crossfire. I mean, there was exchange of fire. Fire was opened from both sides. So there were -- it was very likely that a prisoner might be wounded or killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that one could be killed or wounded. Were they effectively woundings on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: Witness FF
utterances.text: Yes. Quite a number of people were wounded, and some prisoners were killed too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for giving evidence. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will take you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos, are you ready for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The next witness will be examined by my colleague, Mr. Poriouvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to start the examination of our next witness with a private session. The motivation is that now the witness is still occupying some position in Mostar administration, and he lives in Mostar and needs to be protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: My examination will go mostly to the following parts of the indictment: Background, paragraphs 10, 11; Superior Authority, 14, 17; General Allegations, 20, 21; Count 1, 26 through 28, 34(A), (B); Counts 9 through 12, paragraphs 45, 49, 50; Count 18, paragraph 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You told us that you would like to start the examination of your next witness with a private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, with a private session. I will only take some minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. So there are no other protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The witness requested the following protective measures: pseudonym and facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Prosecutor, your request for the protective measures is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go into a private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, just for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, were you ever arrested during the war in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When did it happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us more details? What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: Well, on the 9th of May, 1993, sometime around 5.00 in the morning, my family and I were roused from sleep by intensive gunfire and shelling. So we came out onto the staircase of the building we lived in. All the residents were already awake by then, and nobody could understand what was going on. But be that as it may, after awhile - now, was it one hour or two hours later, I don't know - the first news reached us, I don't even know how, and perhaps I could call it a half information, semi-information, that the HVO was attacking the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then that was confirmed around 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning, when, from the direction of Balinovac, a largish group of citizens turned up. There was my mother, my brother, my sister-in-law, a son of six or five, neighbours; there were children too and elderly, and even a woman who could be around 80. My mother was not much younger; she was around 82. These people turned up and said that they had just been expelled by HVO combatants, by HVO men, who told them to cross to the other side. However, they had already tried to pass through but were turned back by other HVO men, and so they stayed in that building. Perhaps you will want me to tell you what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: First of all, let's stop a little bit. What happened in your area, in your building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: In our building, nothing was happening yet. We were simply in suspense. We did not know what would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, those soldiers you first saw in the adjacent area or your building where you lived.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: When those expelled people arrived, and when we gave them some footwear and some clothes so that they would be covered up, they said that on their heels the HVO soldiers were coming. Then we entered our flats, awaiting what would happen next. After awhile, my flat and other flats were entered by two, three, maybe four soldiers with rifles, with automatic rifles, pointing at me, at my children, my mother; and by that time, my brother and sister-in-law had already arrived, and some other neighbours from Balinovac. They told us to all go out of the building, and we then did go out. There were already some 15 or 20 soldiers by that time there, but they did not allow us to turn around so I couldn't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the soldiers that appeared in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: There were brothers Bajric there, Pehar called Dolma, Vinko Martinovic was turning in front of the building with an automatic, and there were also some others whom I mostly knew by sight only.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But did you know all these personalities you have mentioned? I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mean, Vinko Martinovic, brothers Bajric, and Pehar Dolma. Did you know them before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: I mostly knew them by sight. We did not keep the same company.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What can you tell the Trial Chamber about the actions that were undertaken by these persons, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: There was intimidation. Shots were fired, threats were uttered. For instance, my brother told me how he and his child, who is about five or six years old, how when they came to their flat, they had woken them up because they were still asleep, how they entered with their automatics, pointed their rifles at them and wanted to fire them. And they treated us arrogantly. They treated us just as arrogantly. Whoever was slower amongst us received the blows from those soldiers either with their feet or with a rifle.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you see someone being beaten by anyone from the group of soldiers who came to your building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: No. It would be one or two blows. Perhaps if somebody started to lag behind. It was only when we started off in a column escorted by soldiers towards the Velez stadium under ferocious shelling that we could hear. Stela beckoned a neighbour from the neighbouring building, a journalist from another building and slapped him several times, and then he told him to rejoin the column, and we headed towards the stadium.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did any one of the HVO soldiers explain to you why you were to leave your apartments and to go somewhere to be gathered and transferred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: No. No, nobody. Nobody dared. There were even some threats about killings, about expulsion to Zenica. Well, we did not dare talk to them even, because if any one of us who tried to communicate would be stricken, would receive a blow either on his back or on his head.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber approximately how many people were gathered, I mean in the area of your building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: I'd say -- I'd say about 15 people, from what I could see, but otherwise, I would have to repeat that we were not allowed to turn around much and look around.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And what about your relatives, neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: They were all there. They were all there, relatives, neighbours. Everybody was in this column heading for the stadium. And when I say "all," I also mean my wife, my mother, my brother, my sister-in-law, my two children underage, my brother's small children. We were all in this column heading towards the stadium.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: We were taken towards the Velez stadium, but before the stadium, there is a building. The building, the former command of the JNA, which had subsequently been turned into a university building, and that is where we stopped and where women and children were separated from us. Men were supposed to go on to the Velez stadium, but the trouble started there when they wanted to take along my son as a man, even though he had barely turned 11. They wanted to take him to the stadium. But perhaps because an HVO soldier knew me by sight, we managed also to leave behind my son with my daughter and my wife so that he wouldn't come to the stadium with us, even though my next-door neighbour's son, who was 15 or 16 maybe, did go to the stadium with us as a grown-up man, as an adult. That is, after they had separated, they took women and children apart, we went on and went to the stadium and entered the pitch of the -- of Velez, the soccer club.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How long did they keep you on the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: Well, quite long. Three, four, could have been five hours. I remember well that it was a sunny day and that we had all burnt, that there was no water. An hour or two later, somebody brought a bucket of water. There was quite a large group of people being brought from all over the town.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you eyewitness any facts or mistreatment of detainees on the Velez stadium on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: I did not eyewitness it at the Velez stadium, but I saw man being brought to the stadium who showed signs of harassment. I can mention, for instance, old Professor Badzak, a university professor, who had blood all over him and was bruised. There were other people like that, but I remember him. He was beaten up very badly.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where were you taken from the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: From the stadium -- or rather, the HVO police and the Herceg-Bosna police started to set up groups of about 70 men each. I think that I was in the third or the fourth such group. We were taken to Varda, which is an elevation, a hill above Heliodrom. That is where we were told to get off the buses, and then we set off on foot to the Heliodrom camp.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who received you at the gate of Heliodrom detention facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: Once again, uniformed soldiers. And when we arrived, they took us, or at least my group, they took us to a building called the central prison or something. That is a building made of some solid material with bars on the windows, with a metal door. And I was locked up on the upper floor of that building.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you know what happened to your wife and son, brother and other relatives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: I was told there that they were on the ground floor of the same prison, in that same building. As we were passing by, I could see that there was somebody behind those bars, and those were mostly women. And later on, I had it confirmed that my whole family was right there on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was the central prison the only building where prisoners were kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: No. There were hangars. This was a former airport or heliport, and all these structures were used as a prison. They were all for prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And who was in charge of Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I cannot recall the name of the prison warden.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the names. I'm asking you just had there been sort of a military body that was in charge of Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And who were your guards in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: The HVO police and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Just maybe briefly about the conditions of life for prisoners of Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: I can first tell you personally about my conditions of detention. When we were put on the upper floor, the room that we were in measured 70 square metres. That was written above the door. And we took a count and we are 105. We had a toilet off the hallway, and there was also a metal partition with a metal door. That is what we had. And for the first couple of days, we received no food. Luckily, we had water in that hallway, so that we used it not only to drink but also instead of food. So in that room, there was a little more than one-half square metre per person. That I remember vividly. So I know that when I went to bed, we had to put our smelly shoes - and I apologise for this - under our head. And some people had to step outside and take turns, because we could not all sleep in there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was there any medical assistance at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did any officials from government of Herceg-Bosna ever visit Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: That may have been five or six days later. I don't remember exactly when, but I remember very well the delegation that visited Heliodrom also included the then, I think, Prime Minister. Or he held some very high position in the government of Herceg-Bosna. His last name was Rajic. And I think that I recognised Mr. Greguric, who at that time was the Croatian Prime Minister then. We also had the Minister for Social Affairs or something. His name was Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And was there a change in Heliodrom after their visits?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: At the Heliodrom, the changes only occurred several days later when the ICRC appeared, and that is when the food was brought in. And as far as the visits are concerned, after the visits, they mainly promised us that we would be released but nothing came of it.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you eyewitness any facts of beating of prisoners by some soldiers in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: All I could see is what I saw through the bars when people were brought in or taken away. And those weren't big beatings, but there were kicks and blows by rifle butts and things like that. But I recall very well my first encounter at the Heliodrom. I think this was at the mess hall when we started being taken there to eat, to have something to eat. That mess hall was in the basement of that building. In that encounter I met Fazlija Prguda. He was all swollen from the beatings that he had sustained, and he said that he had been beaten with some hard -- I don't know what. From either a shovel or hoe or something. So he was all beaten up. That was the first time when they had come for him. And I saw him at the Heliodrom. That was on the day before the day when he was beaten for the second time. I also saw other people around, and you could see traces of what I believe were beatings. They had scars and they had hematomas and they had all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know to which unit did the soldiers belong who were involved in the beating of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that? Who took part in it?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know who took part in the beatings of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: At the Heliodrom, I don't know what units they were, but they were basically under the HVO control. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did any other soldiers, apart from those who were guarding the Heliodrom, have access to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: One evening, one could hear terrible noise and argument. There was even some shooting in front of the door where we were, in front and under the window. In the morning, when we woke up and when we established contact with the more moderate ones among the police who were willing to talk to us, they told us that Tuta's soldiers had come, who had been defeated someplace, that they were asking to be given the keys to enter the cells. This was reconfirmed to me by my wife, who also heard it where she was with the women that same night.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did they ever take prisoners to work somewhere outside the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: Yes, there was the first and the second group who were taken away to work. That was in the early days, when there was this terrible hunger, when we were not being given anything to eat. After the first and second group, at the advice of the guards who had entered our cell and other cells, they advised us to always find five or six volunteers because they would fare better, that it was more preferable than the HVO soldiers picking their own choices. So later the guards who guarded us would usually designate five or six persons as volunteers to dig trenches or whatever it was that they were doing. So that later on these people said that, for the most part, they worked on digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And what happened to your relatives in Heliodrom? When were they released from there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: With your permission, can I explain something before I was released? My sister, who was not detained at the Heliodrom camp, found out where we were from television, and this is how it happened: She saw my children playing in front of the prison. Again, if I can just explain a little bit. When some foreign or humanitarian delegations would come, they would bring out the children, and 20 to 50 metres away, there would be -- there would be a vehicle filled with oranges, and the children would be let out to play and then they would be given these oranges or biscuits and things. As soon as the delegation was gone, they would collect them and take them back. All this happened in front of my cell so I could see it from behind the bars, through the window from where I was. And several days later, I don't know exactly, women and children were released.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did they return to your former apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: Yes, they went back to the apartment.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When were you released from the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: On the orders or on the suggestion of General Morillon, I was released after about 15 to 20 days and I went back to my apartment. The apartment was ransacked; the front door was split in two when I came back to the apartment.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you stay in your apartment the rest of the wartime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the witness indicated at the order or suggestion of a gentleman that he was released, and it did not get on the transcript. Line 2. Page 85, line 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you clear it up?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, you just mentioned one gentleman on whose recommendation or order you were released on such occasion from the Heliodrom. Can you repeat your testimony on this issue, because it is not on the transcript. A technical problem.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: It was not General Morillon who was the one who had me released, but it was in agreement with the HVO that all the camps, including the Heliodrom camps, be dissolved. I believe that it was thanks to him, General Morillon, that we were released. Morillon, by the way, is spelled M-o-r-i-l-l-o-n.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did it happen after his visit to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: Yes. He was at the Heliodrom on that day. And let me clarify this right away. As soon as he left, immediately interrogations started and people were again sent back to the cells. I saw him coming to the Heliodrom on that day, and word leaked from the guards and others that he had come precisely in order to effect our release.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You just mentioned that most of the prisoners were interrogated in Heliodrom even after Morillon's visit to Heliodrom. What was the subject matter of that interrogation? What did they want to know from you? What kind of information did they want to get from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: Well, I believe that mostly it had to do with the membership of a unit, where a person lived. But that had no influence of any kind.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you see any military units deployed in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: There were several different kinds of insignia. I know that frequently Mladen Misic, I believe he was commander of the 4th Battalion; through the window I saw Juka Prazina in front of the prison.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you know Juka Prazina before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: No. I only met him sometime in 1992. I think at the time he had -- he killed that young man, Kajan, in Edo Bajram's restaurant. That is a place on the way to the Rondo. But let me just explain this. I did not see him kill this man, but shortly thereafter I saw Juka Prazina, whom I had known by sight, and they told me about him. And I don't know whether he was tried for that murder or not.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But did you see him after the war started, I mean after the 9th of May, or before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: I saw him both before the 9th of May and after the 9th of May. When we were at the Heliodrom, I saw him at the Heliodrom in an HVO uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now let's return to your apartment. You just explained to us that you didn't stay in your apartment until the end of the war, and for some reason left it. Could you explain it to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: I was again expelled from the apartment on the 13th of June. However, before that, they came for me. I think it was about twenty to nine in the evening. There were six HVO soldiers. And I hid at my Croat neighbour's place; until the 13th, I mostly hid at his place. At that point, they took my car away and some belongings from my apartment. Another neighbour from that building next door, who was an ethnic Croat and who was in uniform, called the police. That was again the Herceg-Bosna police. They came, they whispered something to each other, they drove the car away, they took a few things from the house. On the 13th of June, sometime in the afternoon, suddenly the neighbourhood was blocked by 20 to 30 vehicles. I came out to my neighbour's balcony, actually a window. At first we thought that it may have something to do with the burial of the person who had allegedly jumped out the window, a former manager of the AutoPrevoz. At two or three in the morning, he ended up on the pavement; I don't know whether he committed suicide or was thrown out the window. We thought that perhaps this was the burial procession. However, what ensued was expulsion from apartments. Both my brother and I had hidden at my neighbour's, and I was lying between the bed and the window when Ernest Takac burst in, having broken through the door. He, in very insulting language, threatened the neighbour and his wife, saying that they were protecting and hiding balijas. They asked me -- and I hid because I had heard that they were collecting men to use them as human shields, because they were going to try to cross to the east bank. At my neighbour's, my wife, my children, and my mother were also there, and the other members of the family were in my apartment. When they led them away, the column had already formed, and I told my brother, "If they're taking them away, let's join them." So we ran out and we joined them. Ernest Takac approached my brother and started kicking him and hitting him with a rifle butt and other things. And then we started. We started in the direction of the line of separation. We all thought that we were going to be used as human shields. As we were walking, those persons who led us did not allow us to turn to each other and talk. They would shoot at any window where anyone would try to peek out. On the way, they were collecting and rounding up more people. If they were Bosniak -- they were asking questions. If these people were Bosniak, they would be joined in the column and we moved on until we reached the church at Semovac, which is near the line of separation, and they told us, "Go over to your balijas," and we crossed over. That was on the 13th of June, in the afternoon, 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You just gave us the name of a person called Ernest Takac. Do you know him before the 13th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: Also by sight, because he used to come to the neighbourhood in uniform and in civilian clothes. And I remember - this was later, several days before the expulsion - that he even wanted to shoot somebody because of some apartment where a Bosnian had been expelled. And he eventually moved in a colleague of his and threw out another Croat.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was Ernest Takac the only one whom you recognised on the 13th of June as persons who were evicting people from the houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: These were mainly the same persons who were around on the 9th of May, the Bajrics and Pehar and Takac and Nargilic and some others who I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. only knew by sight and who I remembered. Pretty much the same group, though.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: On the 13th of June, you were expelled from the same area as on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG
utterances.text: Yes, from the same apartment, in the same way. Perhaps even worse than on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, my direct is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, because we only have three minutes left, may I suggest that we start tomorrow? Because I don't think there is much use in starting something for two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at 9.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of November, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
